title: What happened to the twelve
hook: church traditions send Thomas to India, Andrew to Greece, James to Spain; tradition says many died as martyrs

segments.voice: Yesterday, Simeon and Anna, waiting in the temple, and your line was the waiting years.

Near the end of Mark's Gospel, the King James Bible gives the mission of the eleven in one line: "And they went forth, and preached every where." A short sentence for a very long road. After it, the New Testament mostly follows Peter and Paul, and the rest of the twelve slip out of the story. Andrew, who went and found his brother Simon. Thomas, who wouldn't believe until he saw the wounds. Bartholomew, Matthew, Thaddaeus, Simon the Canaanite. The Bible doesn't say where they went. But the churches didn't forget, and some still tell which apostle brought them the faith.

The word is tradition: something handed on, from one person to the next. Paul uses it plainly: "hold the traditions which ye have been taught, whether by word, or our epistle." And the stories of the twelve came down mostly by word of mouth. Tradition says Thomas went east as far as India, and Christians in Kerala, in the south of India, call themselves Saint Thomas Christians and trace their church to him. Andrew went to Greece, and Greek tradition remembers his death at Patras. Spanish tradition links James, the brother of John, to Santiago de Compostela, where pilgrims still walk the long road to his shrine. And tradition says many of the twelve died as martyrs. Now the honest part. These are traditions, not chapters of the Bible. Some are old, some grew later, and historians weigh each one on its own. Apart from Judas, Acts tells the death of just one of the twelve, short and hard: Herod "killed James the brother of John with the sword." The same James; Spanish tradition holds his body was carried to Spain afterward. Catholic and Orthodox teaching gives tradition real weight alongside scripture; Protestant churches teach that every tradition is tested by scripture. In Acts, before he is taken up, Jesus says: "ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth." The traditions are a map of people taking that seriously, and some places on that map are still places where being a Christian costs something.
screen: `TO THE UTTERMOST PART OF THE EARTH.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind Christians somewhere who gather quietly because gathering openly isn't safe, or whose church has been burned: a few people, a borrowed room, a door shut before the reading starts. If you pray, pray for them in your own words; if you don't, hold them in your attention, like a friend far away who's having a hard time.
Tradition. Something handed on, by letter or by word of mouth. Here, the stories of where the twelve went, kept by the churches that remember them.
Your line: they went everywhere. The churches still remember who came to them. On we go.

howItsDone: Churches remember the apostles on their feast days, and churches in India, Greece, Spain and elsewhere keep the traditions of the apostles linked to them. Churches also pray, in their services, for Christians who face persecution.

chat.says: Does the Bible say where all twelve apostles went after Jesus?
options: Mostly no. Churches kept the stories as tradition, like Thomas in India.
Yes, Acts follows each of the twelve to the place where they died.
No, and the churches never told any stories about where they went.
chat.meaning: The Bible mostly follows Peter and Paul. Where the rest went came down as tradition: Thomas in India, Andrew in Greece, James linked to Spain.

Kerala.meaning: a region in the south of India

Patras.meaning: a city in Greece where tradition remembers Andrew's death

Santiago de Compostela.meaning: a shrine in Spain that tradition links to James

martyrs.meaning: people who die rather than give up their faith

epistle.meaning: a letter, like Paul's letters to the churches

notes: Editor pass: hook no longer opens on a bare quotation (days 739, 745 and 751 open that way); 'ask in certain towns' softened; practice image adjusted away from day 739's family at a kitchen table.

Mark 16:20 is in the longer ending of Mark (16:9–20), which some early manuscripts lack. The script says only 'a line near the end of Mark's Gospel, in the King James Bible'. Confirm this is acceptable or swap for another verse.

Apostle traditions are all attributed to 'tradition': Thomas in India (Saint Thomas Christians of Kerala), Andrew's death at Patras, James linked to Santiago de Compostela with the tradition that his body was carried to Spain. Confirm wording.

'Tradition says that many of the twelve died as martyrs' follows the index hook ('most, it's said, died as martyrs'), softened from 'most' to 'many' and attributed to tradition. The index hook field was adjusted accordingly; confirm.

Doctrinal summary: 'Catholic and Orthodox teaching gives tradition real weight alongside scripture; Protestant churches teach that every tradition is tested by scripture.' Confirm this is fair to each.
Original: παράδοσις in 2 Thessalonians 2:15 (τὰς παραδόσεις). The gloss 'what is handed on' is the standard lexical sense; confirm.
The list of apostles uses the KJV names (Thaddaeus, Simon the Canaanite) from Mark 3:18.
Second editor pass: 'which apostle walked in first' changed to 'which apostle brought them the faith' (no 'first' claim).
Audit pass: 'Acts does tell one apostle's death' was wrong (Acts 1:18 tells Judas's death); now 'Apart from Judas, Acts tells the death of just one of the twelve'.
